newsitem.title: HONG KONG: H.K. activist feared dead after island protest.
newsitem.headline: H.K. activist feared dead after island protest.

text.p: A Hong Kong protest leader was the focus of a major drama on Thursday when conflicting reports said he was feared to have drowned and others said he had been saved after he staged a protest dive into the East China Sea.

There were confusing reports from Hong Kong radio correspondents aboard the protest ship Kien Hwa 2 about whether David Chan was dead or alive. First aid workers were struggling to revive him, a Hong Kong Cable TV report said.
Hong Kong government radio and Cable TV said earlier that Chan, 45, was feared dead, and that he had no heartbeat or pulse.
Hong Kong Commercial Radio reported that he had been revived but later revised its report, saying he could not swim well, and said that his heart had stopped.

Another activist, Fong Yong-yun, was taken away for medical treatment by a Japanese helicopter and a radio report said he was alive. The two men were among five from Hong Kong who plunged into the sea as part of protest antics against Japan.
"When he (David Chan) was pulled out of the water he had no heartbeat or pulse," Cable TV said.
Japan's Maritime Safety Agency earlier said two men from the Hong Kong ship trying to land on the group of disputed islands were seriously injured after jumping overboard.

The agency said one of the men was taken by helicopter to a hospital in the southern Japanese prefecture of Okinawa and the second was being treated by the Japanese coastguard on the Hong Kong ship. It did not identify them.

"One or two people on board the Hong Kong vessel jumped into the sea and are said to be in serious condition. Our agency's patrol boats have gone to rescue them," a spokesman at Japan's Maritime Safety Agency told Reuters.
He said he had no further details and was still in the process of confirming where the accident occurred.
A Hong Kong radio correspondent on board the rusty tanker Kien Hwa 2 said two of the activists had required first aid and that group leader Chan was unconscious.
They dived from the ship when it was three miles (five km) from the islands, which China calls the Diaoyu group and Japan calls the Senkakus, Hong Kong government radio said.

"They want to demonstrate to the Japanese that Chinese have the right to do whatever they want to do, including swimming in Chinese waters," its correspondent said. The five activists were wearing lifejackets, the radio added.
The tanker was surrounded by 20 Japanese vessels, five planes and one helicopter, he said.
Earlier in the day, stormy seas forced the protest ship, which set sail from Hong Kong last Sunday, to abandon efforts to plant the Chinese flag on the islands.

But the Kien Hwa 2 carrying 18 demonstrators again sailed close to the disputed chain of islands and activists staged the protest dives into the sea in a bid to further harry Japan and keep the international spotlight on the quarrel.

Yuta Enomoto, public relations officer at Japan's Maritime Safety Agency told Reuters: "Yes, the Hong Kong ship entered Japanese waters early Thursday morning. It left (Japanese waters) once around 5 a.m. but returned again around 9 a.m."
"We used radio transmission for the Hong Kong vessel and loud speakers for the Taiwanese boats to warn them to leave Japanese waters."
Correspondents on board the ship said the protesters had abandoned landing efforts because of bad weather and high waves.
"The ship's captain said high waves made landing impossible so they abanboned the plan," it said.

The protesters had hoped symbolically to reclaim the isles from Japan by removing Japanese flags and a lighthouse erected by Japanese ultra-nationalists in July, and by raising China's five-star red communist flag.
